title: 8th Sitting of first Session of 2025
summary: The sitting opened at 09:02 with 38 members present. The main business was the no-confidence motion against the Minister of Homeland Security and Technology, Ali Ihsan, brought by 12 MDP members over a foreign-worker management system contract, alleged political influence on police investigations, and use of the national registration database to add members to the PNC. The minister answered at length and rejected the claims, then MDP, MDA and PNC members debated it, with repeated points of order and a member being told to leave the chamber; the debate was closed with the vote left for the day's vote time. After a recess the House began the opening debate on a bill to amend the Courts Act on the Supreme Court bench, which was still being debated when this part ends. This part continues the first debate on a bill by Holhudhoo MP Abdul Sattar Mohamed to amend the Courts Act (Law 22/2010), which would shrink the Supreme Court bench and so remove two sitting judges. MDP members argued it conflicts with the Constitution and pressures a pending Supreme Court case; PNC members said the Constitution does not fix the bench size and that it is a member's bill, not the government's. After a recess the sponsor closed the debate and the Majlis accepted the bill 64-12 and sent it to the Judiciary Committee; it also rejected a no-confidence motion against the Homeland Security Minister, 11 for and 64 against.

speakers.name: Ali Ihsan
positions: Said the expatriate system dates back to 2012 and a 2016 agreement, and that earlier governments received the company's claims, including US$13.7 million, without acting on them.
Said political staff did party-form work inside the DNR office, called it unwise, said he has ordered it not to happen again, and put the forms at about 1,700.
Cited drug seizures, ID card and police-station rollout and deportations, and denied that he interfered in police investigations.

speakers.name: Meekail Ahmed Nasym
positions: Raised repeated points of order, objecting to the minister's remarks about the DNR forms and photos and asking that the chair apply points-of-order rules consistently.
Was named by the chair after three warnings and asked to leave the chamber.

speakers.name: Dr. Ahmed Shamheed
positions: Cited Bangladeshi and Malaysian news reports about the company's owners and an extradition request, linking them to the Bestinet system.
Said the December 2024 Majlis decision treated settlement agreements made outside legal process as invalid, and questioned the minister's loss figures.
Estimated about US$150 million would be charged to roughly 30,000 workers at US$5,000 each under the arrangement.
Said the amendment contradicts Article 154 (judges' removal) and Article 142 of the Constitution, which bars interference with the courts.

speakers.name: Ibrahim Shujau
positions: Raised a point of order saying opposition members were unwilling to listen to the minister's answers.
In debate, said the minister had answered every point, that the opposition figures were unsupported, and that the motion was political.
Supported the amendment and said PNC's parliamentary group backs it.
Traced earlier changes to the Supreme Court bench size (2010, 2014, 19th Majlis) and said opposition criticism of this one was misplaced.

speakers.name: Hussain Sameer
positions: Said the bill conflicts with Article 154 of the Constitution, which protects judges from removal except through set procedures; urged members to vote it out.
Asked how judges could suddenly be unfit after the Judicial Service Commission and Majlis approved them, and said past rulings could then be questioned.
Said members' oath is to uphold the Constitution, which should outweigh any party or whip instruction.

speakers.name: Ibrahim Nazil
positions: Raised a point of order asking the minister to give the dates of the Attorney General and controller letters he cited.
Said the settlement worth about MVR 6.9 billion over 15 years was reached outside legal process and that the minister had not answered the questions put to him.
Recalled that members of the 18th Majlis who acted on the courts later had to go to court themselves, and urged careful thought.
Said he did not want any court or president to become the most powerful, and wanted existing laws and the Constitution followed.

speakers.name: Ameen Faisal
positions: Presented the motion, saying the minister breached constitutional duties by handing the expatriate system to a blacklisted Malaysian company on a MVR 460 million a year contract.
Said the minister obstructed police investigations of government-linked people, and that the DNR database was used to fill PNC membership forms without people's consent.
Said the Supreme Court is the institution the public trusts most and its bench should not change overnight, despite the Majlis majority.
Objected to the five-day timeline and said two judges without any fault would be removed regardless.

speakers.name: Ahmed Nazim
positions: Said the motion shows nothing proving a breach of Article 132, and expressed full confidence in the minister's work on drugs, foreign workers and corruption.
On the Courts bill, supported it, saying the Majlis may set the court's composition by law and that recent concerns about the Supreme Court bench justify acting.

speakers.name: Hussain Ziyad
positions: Said the minister's own answers confirmed that DNR data and photos were used in party forms, which he described as a serious concern.
Criticised the size of the cabinet and said ministers should be held accountable.
Questioned why any president needs this much power and said political fortunes change, so the Majlis should weigh the consequences.
Said the number of Supreme Court judges can legally be changed and he was not opposing for its own sake.

speakers.name: Hussain Shareef
positions: Defended the minister, citing the government's work on corruption, drugs, foreign workers and public safety.
Asked which government had stopped settlement-agreement payments, arguing the previous MDP government created committees and paid them.

speakers.name: Abdul Sattar Mohamed
positions: Introduced the bill to amend the Courts Act on the Supreme Court bench and removal process, citing the Majlis's constitutional power to amend laws.
Said there is never a moment with no case before some court, so pending cases cannot bar amending a law.
Said MDP's criticisms lacked legal basis and asked for the bill to pass quickly and be reviewed in committee.

speakers.name: Abdul Gafoor Moosa
positions: Said the proposed Courts Act amendment is a bad one, calling the Supreme Court the one remaining hope of citizens; his turn continues into part 2.
Opposed the bill; said the Supreme Court works for the public good and order, and replacing it would leave the country without recourse.
Argued that if the Supreme Court has made no mistake, the Majlis should not use legislation to replace its judges.

speakers.name: Mohamed Ibrahim
positions: Cited President Muizzu's earlier statements and campaign book as a pledge not to interfere with the judiciary.
Asked why a PNC-linked member tabled the bill while a sensitive Supreme Court case is under way, and whether the President approved it.

speakers.name: Ahmed Didi
positions: Called the bill an attempt to influence the courts while a Supreme Court case linked to the Majlis is under way; opposed it.
Noted PNC's parliamentary group leader had said weeks earlier that the Supreme Court bench would not be changed.

speakers.name: Mauroof Zakir
positions: Said the bill, tabled while a Supreme Court case on MPs' seats is pending, amounts to an attempt to influence that case.
Noted differing views even among PNC members and asked why the bench would change suddenly if the goal were wider judicial reform.

speakers.name: Mohamed Ismail
positions: Supported the amendment and said the opposition's objections do not address its content.
Pointed to MDP-era treatment of judges and the courts in answer to the opposition's criticism.

speakers.name: Mohamed Abbas
positions: Said his party, the MDA, has full confidence in the minister, citing drug enforcement, ID cards and police stations on islands.
Said the motion was an attempt to hide past governments' wrongdoing and that ministers must be allowed to answer in the House.

speakers.name: Hassan Zareer
positions: Said the minister's reply left the opposition with little to rebut and called the motion political.
Said the government has deported thousands of irregular foreign workers and cited fewer irregular migrants in Hulhumale' as results.

speakers.name: Hussain Imran Latheef
positions: Raised a point of order saying there is no evidence the President would interfere with the courts, and objected to discussing someone absent.

speakers.name: Ibrahim Falah
positions: Clarified, on a point of order, that the bill was tabled by a member and is not a government bill.

speakers.name: Mohamed Niushad
positions: Raised a point of order that MDP members were present in the chamber, after a speaker said they were absent.

speakers.name: Abdul Rahman
positions: Traced the bench from seven judges to five (2014) and back to seven (2019), questioned what changing it again would achieve, and opposed the bill.
Recalled voters backed the President on a pledge not to use the courts, and said the bill runs against that promise.

speakers.name: Ahmed Thariq
positions: Supported the bill; recalled a 2019 placard calling for former Chief Justice Abdulla Saeed's release as an example of politics affecting the judiciary.
Said the Constitution does not fix the Supreme Court bench size, so the Majlis majority may set it at 5, 9, 11 or other numbers.

decisions: Economic Committee deadline of 25 March 2025 announced for the motion on a grooming and dress standard for resort and hotel staff
Chair ruled no urgent matter could be taken while a no-confidence vote on a minister is under way
Chair named South Galolhu member Meekail Ahmed Nasym after three warnings and asked him to leave the chamber
Chair closed debate on the no-confidence motion against Minister Ali Ihsan and set the vote for the day's vote time
Sitting recessed from 10:30 to 11:00 and resumed with the preliminary debate on the Courts Act amendment bill
Bill to amend the Courts Act (Law 22/2010) accepted at first stage by 64 votes to 12.
Bill sent to the Judiciary Committee for review under Rule 106(r) of the Majlis rules.
No-confidence motion against Homeland Security and Technology Minister Ali Ihusaan did not pass (11 yes, 64 no, 47 needed).
Next sitting set for Wednesday 26 February 2025 at 9:00.

votes.what: No-confidence motion against Minister of Homeland Security and Technology Ali Ihusaan (47 votes needed)
Accepting the bill to amend the Courts Act (Law 22/2010) (39 votes needed)
